prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: the optical lattice clock alone, credited to Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange tested it on the points that matter to me and it held. Nature supplies the magic-wavelength condition, which cancels the trapping Stark shift and lets very many neutral atoms be interrogated at once; the instrument built on that idea has been reproduced across several laboratories and compared across continents at uncertainties near 1e-18. The consequences are concrete and already in use: preparation for the redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, and limits on varying constants and dark-sector couplings. It is also the only shortlisted case in which the credit question is small. The remaining candidates each have a real attribution problem. I withdrew my own opening first choice, the CMB acoustic-peak programme (B008), because three seats cannot cover COBE-era, WMAP, Planck and the early acoustic-oscillation theory without settling a priority question by fiat. I do not treat the eight-member overlap in opening rankings as evidence of merit. I treat it as a reason to check whether we are choosing a safe compromise, and on the science I do not think we are.
statement.case_against: The overlap with earlier prizes is the objection I take most seriously, and I do not consider it fully answered. The 2005 prize covered the comb and laser precision spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize covered control of single quantum systems, including the ion-clock lineage. A reader could call the lattice clock an extension of both. I think it is a distinct invention, because the many-atom magic-wavelength concept solves a different problem from the single-ion approach, but that is a judgment and the citation has to carry it. A two-name credit also omits Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups. Several of us, me included, are judging Katori's priority against Ye's development from general knowledge and not from verified records. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the downstream case is still prospective.

responses.point: You and I both argue that the lattice clock is a different concept from the comb and ion-clock prizes, and you add a 1e-18 clause to the citation.
responses.response: I accept your 1e-18 clause and have adopted it, with one condition. The clause should follow the invention itself and not replace it, so that the citation names the lattice clock first and the accuracy second. A citation that leads with a measurement level reads as a prize for precision spectroscopy in general, which is the territory 2005 and 2012 covered. I also share your caveat that priority between Katori's proposal and parallel work rests on recollection. I would not make that a reason to delay, but I would want the committee's external experts to confirm the sequence of the proposal and first strontium realisation before the vote.

responses.point: You prefer topological insulators (B019) with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a prediction confirmed by experiment, and you consider the timing right after nearly two decades of confirmation.
responses.response: Your maturity argument is stronger than I credited in round 1. Nearly two decades of independent confirmation across material families is real, and the Kane and Mele Z2 result is a genuine conceptual step. It remains my first alternative. Where I still differ is attribution. You concede that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang pointed Molenkamp to HgTe, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and the Bi2Se3 experiments is also missing. A trio therefore decides a contested priority question. The 2016 prize on topological phases narrows the novelty further. The lattice clock has an open boundary too, but it is at the edge of the field, whereas here it runs through the middle of the claim. I would reconsider if the committee's experts can show a citation that honours the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation without implying the credit is complete.

responses.point: You moved the lattice clock to the head of your list and now treat the Higgs discovery (B054) as an alternative, while stating that the Higgs attribution problem is no better resolved than the clock's.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning on the Higgs. It is the most consequential outstanding experimental result in particle physics, and my objection was never to its weight. The difficulty is that any trio from Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee leaves out colleagues with equal claims, and I do not see a wording that avoids that. On IceCube I still agree that the diffuse flux is established and that Halzen and Karle are a credible pair. We both noted that individual source identification is thin and that AMANDA and Baikal precursors are not credited, so I keep it as the second alternative and not as a lead. I have no objection to you handling the chair's connections to B033 and B054 by recusal discussion if either is ever advanced, and none is needed for B048.

responses.point: You judge the demonstrated impact of the lattice clock to outweigh the timing argument about the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I now side with you on timing. In round 1 I listed the unfinished redefinition as an open uncertainty. Waiting would change the framing but not the science. The invention is done, it has been reproduced independently, and the redefinition is a consequence of that work, not a condition for it. Our task is to recognise the discovery, and the Academy has recognised foundational work before its largest application arrived. I would only ask that the citation not claim the redefinition as an achievement. That is why I prefer wording that ends at the 1e-18 level and leaves the SI second out of the text.

responses.point: You see no natural fit for a second prize part alongside the clock within the three-laureate limit.
responses.response: I agree. The chair asked whether a second part such as trapped-ion quantum logic (B003) should accompany B048. Adding one leaves a single place for a part that has three credited names, so it forces an arbitrary exclusion among Cirac, Zoller and Blatt, and it dilutes a prize that is strongest as one clear invention. I therefore keep to a single achievement and two laureates. I also take your caution that broad support is not a merit argument, and I have tried to argue the case on the science in this round and not on counts.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes; my view is that it is, but I regard this as the central judgment and not a settled point.
Whether Katori and Ye alone fairly cover the invention given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups, and whether the priority sequence I am recalling is correct.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second would, once adopted, strengthen the citation enough to justify waiting; I currently think it would not.
Whether the missing credit for Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang makes B019 unworkable as a fallback.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My documented connections (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not involve any credited name on this shortlist. My own field is string theory and cosmology, so I remain an outsider on the atomic-physics and condensed-matter cases, and my judgment of the lattice clock rests on the committee record and general knowledge, not on field expertise. I have no conflict with the flags raised by others and see no need for recusal on B048.
